questions.question: A reaction has $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$. Assuming $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ do not change with temperature, under which condition is the reaction spontaneous at constant pressure?
options: Only at high temperatures, above $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$
Only at low temperatures, below $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$

solution.key_concept: Spontaneity at constant T and p is decided by the sign of $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$.
steps: Here $\Delta H > 0$ works against spontaneity, while $-T\Delta S < 0$ works for it.
The $T\Delta S$ term becomes larger than $\Delta H$ only when T is high enough.
So $\Delta G < 0$ only when $T > \Delta H/\Delta S$.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Only at high temperatures, above $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$
solution.why_not_others: Spontaneity at all temperatures needs $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$. Spontaneity at no temperature needs $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S < 0$. Spontaneity only at low temperatures needs both $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ to be negative.
solution.common_trap: Assuming an endothermic reaction can never be spontaneous.
solution.time_saving_tip: When $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ have the same sign, the sign of $\Delta S$ tells you whether the reaction is favoured at high or low temperature.

questions.question: For a reaction, $\Delta H = +180\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ and $\Delta S = +150\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$. Assuming both values are independent of temperature, the reaction is spontaneous:

solution.key_concept: Crossover temperature $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$, with both quantities in the same energy unit.
steps: Convert $\Delta H$ to joules: $\Delta H = 180000\ J\ mol^{-1}$.
Calculate the crossover temperature: $T = 180000/150 = 1200\ K$.
Both $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ are positive, so $\Delta G < 0$ only above 1200 K.
solution.why_not_others: 1.2 K comes from leaving $\Delta H$ in kJ while $\Delta S$ is in J. 927 K wrongly subtracts 273 from a temperature that is already in kelvin. 'Below 1200 K' reverses the direction that applies when $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ are both positive.
solution.common_trap: Mixing kJ and J when calculating $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$.

questions.question: For a process at 250 K and constant pressure, $\Delta H_{sys} = -50\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ and $\Delta S_{sys} = -150\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$. The total entropy change of the universe and the Gibbs energy change of the process are, respectively:

steps: Add the system term: $\Delta S_{total} = -150 + 200 = +50\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$.
Then $\Delta G = -T\Delta S_{total} = -250 \times 50 = -12500\ J\ mol^{-1} = -12.5\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) takes $\Delta S_{surr}$ with the wrong sign. Option (2) treats $\Delta S_{sys}$ as positive. Option (3) drops the minus sign in $\Delta G = -T\Delta S_{total}$.
solution.common_trap: Writing $\Delta S_{surr} = +\Delta H_{sys}/T$ instead of $-\Delta H_{sys}/T$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Once you have $\Delta S_{total} > 0$, $\Delta G$ must be negative, which eliminates options (1) and (3) straight away.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: A reaction with $\Delta G < 0$ at constant temperature and pressure may still proceed at an extremely slow rate.
statements.R: The decrease in Gibbs energy, $-\Delta G$, equals the maximum useful (non-pV) work that can be obtained from a process.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Spontaneity criteria say nothing about rate, and $-\Delta G$ is the maximum non-expansion work.
steps: A is true because $\Delta G < 0$ only shows that a reaction is spontaneous; it says nothing about its rate.
R is true because $-\Delta G = w_{useful,max}$.
R describes the work interpretation of $\Delta G$. It does not explain why a spontaneous reaction can be slow.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: R is not the reason for A; the correct explanation is that thermodynamics does not predict rate. Both statements are true, so options (3) and (4) are wrong.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that a negative $\Delta G$ means a fast reaction.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: At constant temperature and pressure, $\Delta G = -T\Delta S_{total}$, so a positive entropy change of the universe necessarily corresponds to a negative Gibbs energy change of the system.
statements.II: For a reaction with $\Delta H = -120\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ and $\Delta S = -300\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$ (both independent of temperature), $\Delta G$ is negative at 300 K but positive at 500 K.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: $\Delta G = -T\Delta S_{total}$; when $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ are both negative, the reaction is spontaneous only below $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$.
steps: Statement I: T is always positive, so $\Delta S_{total} > 0$ gives $\Delta G < 0$. Statement I is correct.
Statement II, crossover temperature: $T = 120000/300 = 400\ K$.
At 300 K: $\Delta G = -120 + 300(0.300) = -30\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$, which is negative.
At 500 K: $\Delta G = -120 + 500(0.300) = +30\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$, which is positive. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements check out by calculation, so every option that marks either statement incorrect is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Assuming an exothermic reaction is spontaneous at every temperature.
solution.time_saving_tip: Find the crossover temperature (400 K) first. If both $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ are negative, the reaction is spontaneous below it and non-spontaneous above it.

questions.question: For a reaction at 298 K, the standard Gibbs energy change $\Delta_r G^\circ$ is positive. Which of the following is correct about its equilibrium constant K?

steps: If $\Delta_r G^\circ > 0$, then $\ln K < 0$.
This means $0 < K < 1$, so the equilibrium mixture favours reactants.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): K < 1 and reactants are favoured
solution.why_not_others: K > 1 requires a negative $\Delta_r G^\circ$. K = 1 requires $\Delta_r G^\circ = 0$. K is an exponential, $K = e^{-\Delta_r G^\circ/RT}$, so it can never be negative.
solution.common_trap: Confusing a negative $\ln K$ with a negative K.

questions.question: The equilibrium constant of a reaction at 298 K is $1.0 \times 10^{3}$. What is the standard Gibbs energy change of the reaction? ($R = 8.314\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$)

steps: Calculate $2.303RT = 2.303 \times 8.314 \times 298 \approx 5706\ J\ mol^{-1}$.
Here $\log K = 3$.
So $\Delta_r G^\circ = -5706 \times 3 = -17117\ J\ mol^{-1} \approx -17.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.
solution.why_not_others: $+17.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ has the wrong sign, since K > 1 requires a negative $\Delta_r G^\circ$. $-7.43\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ leaves out the factor 2.303. $-17117\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ labels a value in joules as kJ.
solution.common_trap: Using $\log K$ with $RT$ instead of $2.303RT$, or mixing up J and kJ.
solution.time_saving_tip: At 298 K, $\Delta G^\circ$ changes by about 5.7 kJ for every factor of 10 in K, so $\Delta G^\circ \approx -3 \times 5.7 = -17.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.

questions.question: For a gas-phase reaction at 298 K, $\Delta H^\circ = +3.5\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = +50\ J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}$. Taking $2.303RT = 5.7\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ at 298 K, the equilibrium constant of the reaction is approximately:

steps: Calculate $T\Delta S^\circ = 298 \times 0.050 = 14.9\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.
Then $\Delta G^\circ = 3.5 - 14.9 = -11.4\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.
Therefore $K = 10^2 = 100$.
solution.why_not_others: 0.01 comes from a sign error in $\Delta G^\circ$. 4.6 is the value of $\ln K$, not K. 2 is the value of $\log K$, not K.
solution.common_trap: Stopping at $\log K$ or $\ln K$ and reporting it as K.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Tenfold increase in K at 298 K

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: $\Delta_r G^\circ$ lowered by about $5.7\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$

solution.key_concept: $\Delta_r G = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ and $\Delta_r G^\circ = -2.303RT\log K$
steps: A: a negative $\Delta_r G^\circ$ gives K > 1, so A matches III.
B: $\Delta_r G^\circ = 0$ gives K = 1, so B matches I.
C: at equilibrium $\Delta_r G = 0$ and Q = K, so C matches IV.
D: since $2.303RT \approx 5.7\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$, each tenfold increase in K lowers $\Delta_r G^\circ$ by about 5.7 kJ, so D matches II.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) swaps K = 1 and K > 1. Option (2) wrongly treats every equilibrium as having K = 1, i.e. $\Delta_r G^\circ = 0$. Option (4) assigns the 5.7 kJ shift to A.
solution.common_trap: Believing that $\Delta G^\circ = 0$ at every equilibrium.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Gibbs energy and the equilibrium constant are correct?

statements.A: At equilibrium $\Delta_r G = 0$, but $\Delta_r G^\circ$ is generally not zero.
statements.B: If equal concentrations of N and D exist at equilibrium in $N \rightleftharpoons D$ at temperature T, then $\Delta S^\circ = \Delta H^\circ/T$.
statements.C: Since $\Delta_r G = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln Q$, $\Delta_r G$ is negative whenever Q < K.
statements.D: A reaction with $K = 10^{-3}$ at 298 K has $\Delta_r G^\circ \approx -17.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.

solution.key_concept: $\Delta_r G = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln Q$, which can be written as $RT\ln(Q/K)$.
steps: A is correct: $\Delta G^\circ$ is zero only when K = 1.
B is correct: equal concentrations give K = 1, so $\Delta G^\circ = 0$ and $\Delta H^\circ = T\Delta S^\circ$.
C is correct: substituting $\Delta_r G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ gives $\Delta_r G = RT\ln(Q/K)$, which is negative when Q < K.
D is incorrect: $\Delta_r G^\circ = -5.7 \times (-3) = +17.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and C only
solution.why_not_others: D has the wrong sign, which rules out options (3) and (4). Option (2) leaves out C, which is correct.
solution.common_trap: Getting the sign of $\Delta G^\circ$ wrong when K < 1.
solution.time_saving_tip: K < 1 always means a positive $\Delta G^\circ$, so D can be rejected without any calculation.
